split.name_en: Torah study as an alternative to military service
split.plus_en: Torah study recognized as service that replaces army service
split.minus_en: Torah study gives no exemption from army service
split.statement_en: Full-time Torah study should be recognized by law as service to the state, even if more yeshiva students do not serve in the army.

split.plus_en: wider civilian-service options and exemptions for conscientious objectors
split.minus_en: army service with fewer civilian alternatives or exemptions
split.statement_en: People who cannot or will not serve in the army, including conscientious objectors, should be offered civilian service instead, even if fewer people enlist.

reason: Statement joins Torah study (78% of weight, Basic Law vote) with conscientious objection and civilian service: different issues backed by opposite camps, so one answer cannot cover both.
Weighty bills require or encourage women's representation on Knesset lists, local councils, planning and religious bodies; the statement matches. Only light bills are off-topic.

statements.new_statement_en: Unemployment benefits should cover more people, such as the self-employed, medical interns, young workers and people in job training, even if National Insurance spends more.

reason: Bills extend unemployment benefits to the listed groups and also to young workers (age 18-19) and parents; broaden the examples. Flag-law bills are off-topic.

split.plus_en: stricter licensing, fewer civilians allowed to carry guns
split.minus_en: easier licensing, more civilians allowed to carry guns
split.statement_en: Gun licenses for civilians should be harder to get, even if fewer people can carry a gun for self-defense.

split.plus_en: harsher criminal law against illegal weapons and armed groups
split.minus_en: milder criminal law on illegal weapons
split.statement_en: Possessing or trading illegal weapons should carry much harsher penalties, even if more people go to prison for longer.

reason: Two distinct issues joined by «and»: who may get a gun license, and penalties for illegal weapons. Many voters want easier licenses and tougher enforcement, so positions blur.
The heaviest bills dismiss teachers, lecturers and civil servants who support terror; the statement matches. Bills on senior officials, police suspension and sex offenders are off-topic.
Nearly all bills freeze or deduct funds Israel transfers to the Palestinian Authority over terror payments; the statement matches. Only the false-complaints bills are off-topic.
Bills expand benefits for widows, widowers, orphans and bereaved military families (a few restrict them); the statement matches.

split.name_en: Immunity of soldiers and police for operational actions
split.plus_en: more immunity from prosecution or investigation
split.minus_en: full criminal accountability for operational actions
split.statement_en: Soldiers and police should have immunity from prosecution for actions during operations, even if some abuses go unpunished.

split.name_en: Powers of security agencies over civilians
split.plus_en: wider search, data and protection powers for security agencies
split.statement_en: Police, prison and security services should get wider powers, such as searches and access to personal data, even if this limits citizens' privacy.

reason: Immunity bills carry under a third of the weight; the heaviest bills are about ministers' access to secret information, prison-service privacy exemption, search powers and protecting bases.

split.name_en: Ban on conversion therapy for minors
split.statement_en: Therapy aimed at changing a minor's sexual orientation should be banned by law, even if some parents want it for their children.

split.plus_en: more services, refunds and rights for patients
split.minus_en: fewer obligations on health funds and providers
split.statement_en: Health funds should owe patients more services and rights, such as treatment within a set time and ambulance refunds, even if health insurance costs rise.

split.name_en: Bringing food into hospitals on Passover
split.plus_en: patients and visitors may bring any food into hospitals
split.minus_en: hospitals may ban leavened food on Passover
split.statement_en: Patients and visitors should be allowed to bring any food into hospitals during Passover, even if this conflicts with kosher rules there.

reason: Three separate issues carry the weight: conversion-therapy ban (LGBT/religion), health-fund services (spending), Passover food in hospitals (religion and state). The current statement already joins two.

split.name_en: Cameras to protect children and vulnerable people in care
split.plus_en: mandatory cameras in daycare, kindergartens, special education and geriatric wards
split.minus_en: no mandatory cameras in care settings
split.statement_en: Cameras should be required in daycare centers, kindergartens and special education classes, even if this intrudes on staff privacy.

split.name_en: Filming police use of force at protests
split.plus_en: mandatory video of water cannons and crowd-control means
split.minus_en: no duty to film police crowd control
split.statement_en: Police should be required to film every use of water cannons and other crowd-control means at protests, even if this burdens police work.

split.name_en: Broadcasting court hearings and public meetings
split.plus_en: courts and public bodies recorded and broadcast
split.statement_en: Court hearings and local council meetings should be filmed and broadcast to the public, even if this exposes the privacy of those involved.

reason: Three different issues: cameras protecting children in care, filming police crowd control, broadcasting courts and councils. They draw different camps; the current statement joins two with «and».
Weighty bills impose environmental rules: climate law, bag levy, tree and coast protection, fishing, recycling, pollution. The statement matches.
Most weight is on limiting cut-offs, travel bans, seizures and payment demands on debtors, including reservists; the statement matches. Collecting military-court compensation is off-topic.

split.minus_en: cannabis legal and regulated for personal use
split.statement_en: Cannabis should be legal for personal use, even if drug use may increase.

split.plus_en: alcohol sales restricted to licensed outlets
split.minus_en: supermarkets may sell wine and alcohol
split.statement_en: Large supermarkets should be allowed to sell wine and other alcoholic drinks, even if alcohol becomes easier to buy.

reason: Cannabis bills dominate, but alcohol sales in large stores and tobacco enforcement carry about a third of the weight and divide voters differently. Tobacco left out.
Electronic monitoring under protective orders carries most weight; the statement matches. The organized-crime law is one heavy off-topic bill; the rest are light.

split.plus_en: more free education services from early childhood to university
split.statement_en: The state should provide more free education, from early childhood and after-school programs to university, even if this requires more public spending.

split.plus_en: a Haredi track inside the state school system
split.minus_en: Haredi schooling stays outside state education
split.statement_en: The state should open a Haredi stream within state education, even if it competes with existing independent Haredi school networks.

reason: The heaviest bills create a Haredi state-education stream, a distinct issue. Others expand free services, including universities and tuition, beyond the current examples.

split.minus_en: prime minister limited in consecutive terms
split.statement_en: A prime minister should be limited to two consecutive terms, even if voters lose the option to re-elect a popular leader.

split.name_en: Fixed terms for Supreme Court justices
split.statement_en: Supreme Court justices should serve a fixed number of years rather than until retirement age, even if experienced judges must leave earlier.

split.plus_en: indicted prime minister or ministers may stay in office
split.minus_en: indicted prime minister or ministers must leave office
split.statement_en: A prime minister or minister charged with a crime should have to leave office, even before a court rules on guilt.

reason: Statement joins two ideas pushed by opposite camps: PM term limits and fixed terms for justices. Indictment-removal bills form a third distinct issue.
